correctness.rationale: Every nonempty subset of [n] with gcd g is g times a gcd-one subset of [floor(n/g)], so count f(floor(n/g)). The complement deficits also include the empty subset, yielding A=1+sum_{g>=2,g not dividing n} f(floor(n/g)) and B=1+sum_{g>=2,gcd(g,n)>1} f(floor(n/g)). The smallest admissible gcd is a(n) in A and least prime p(n) in B. Subsets containing 1 give 2^(m-1)<=f(m)<=2^m-1, so the first term controls each sum below and at most n+1 such terms control above; dividing the positive bounds proves exact factor 2(n+1) sandwich. For even n, p=2,a>=3 so h<=floor(n/3)-n/2; for odd n a=2,p>=3 so h>=floor(n/2)-floor(n/3). Exponential gaps dominate the factor n. Independently computed f by the gcd decomposition recurrence, then A,B and both rational inequalities for all 4<=n<=150 in exact integers. The infinite argument is analytic/combinatorial, not finite enumeration.
residual_risks: Only a factor-polynomial sandwich, not a constant-relative asymptotic; other partial-sum questions are untreated.

value.rationale: The paper introducing D and Phi explicitly raised these two extremal complementary-deficit limits. Resolving a precise published open quantitative question and giving a uniform pointwise arithmetic exponent h(n) is a motivated and potentially reusable invariant, beyond an elementary parity sign. Its proof is short but the result is genuinely a sharp qualitative even/odd separation and not merely a recomputation of known D(n) tables.
residual_risks: The multiplicative factor 2(n+1) prevents claiming exact asymptotic constants; historical priority bounded by inspected sources.

final_claim: For n>=4, with D(n)=sum_{d|n} f(d), Phi(n) counting nonempty subsets of [n] whose gcd is coprime to n, a(n)=least g>=2 not dividing n, p(n)=smallest prime factor and h(n)=floor(n/a(n))-floor(n/p(n)), the deficit quotient (2^n-D(n))/(2^n-Phi(n)) lies between 2^h/[2(n+1)] and 2(n+1)2^h. It tends to zero along even n and diverges along odd n, resolving Pongsriiam 2013 Question 3.3.
